place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the notice board

setup.zh: 外门的告示栏上，贴着一张新的告示，墨迹还没干：沉鼎秘境，十年一开。冬月初一，外门弟子皆可入。
setup.en: On the outer court's notice board, a new notice, the ink not yet dry: the Chending Secret Realm opens once in ten years. On the first of the eleventh month, all outer disciples may enter.

story.zh:
周衡合上账簿，叹了口气，自言自语地道：「修仙最要紧的是不丢东西。」也不知是说给谁听的。他临走的时候，从袖子里摸出一根蜡烛，当着一屋子新弟子的面，「咔」地掰成两截，一截放在门边的窗台上，一截揣回了袖子里，道：「灯油，一个月半根。省着点用。」

发完了东西，便开饭。外门的饭堂是一间长长的矮屋，一排长桌，一排长凳，一口大锅。掌勺的是个胖大的伙夫，一人一勺糙米粥，一碟咸菜，一只粗瓷碗。饿了一整天的一百来个孩子，扑到桌子跟前，稀里呼噜，满屋子都是喝粥的声音，倒像下了一场急雨。

小满记着舅舅那三条规矩的第三条，喝得比谁都快。一碗粥喝完了，他把碗捧起来，把碗底舔得干干净净，这才放下。

放下了，他又拿起来。

那是一只粗瓷碗，灰白的，碗口上一道青边，平平常常，外门饭堂里这样的碗，少说也有两三百只。可这一只，碗沿上一个缺口也没有。

小满捧着它，看了很久。他想起家里那四只碗，想起碎在地上的那七八片，想起他娘蹲在地上，一片一片地捡，捡起来拿布包好，放进箱子里。他不知道他娘留着那一包碎片做什么。他也没有问过。

话分两头。

外门女弟子的大通铺，在另一个院子里。那一夜，大通铺上鼾声也是一片，只最靠墙的一张铺上，有一盏豆大的油灯还亮着。灯底下趴着一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘，红鼻头，拿一截新削的炭条，在一个巴掌大的小本子上，一笔一画地写。

她写的是：

九月初九。重阳。

石阶。三百级。冲上去的，没坐。脚底磨了两个泡，记：左一，右一。

他在后头，走的，不跑。三步一口气，像他爹。一百六十级那里，他扭头看了一眼石壁。没停。

洛书。我摆好的时候，他还在发呆。后来他摆对了。比我慢半炷香。记：他娘教的。我娘没教过我这个。

林子。那东西九个头。我是闭着眼睛走过去摸的树皮，没看它。他看了，还扔了石头。他往右滚那一下，我没看懂，像是有人跟他说了什么。记：问。不问。先记着。

测灵石。我，三种，他们说中上。他，五种，他们笑。我没笑。马小宝笑了三声，记：三声。

他没认出我。

娘说：去。娘说：别跟他一路走。一个人去会死，两个人一起去，死一双，不划算。娘说完就哭了。爹送我走的小路，比他们晚到一天，住在庙廊底下。

记：娘，欠我一个不哭。

爹背我走了一段。过了老槐树，爹说：「过了这棵树，就不是咱村了。」他把我放下来，让我自己走。我回头看了一眼。那棵树，我在树底下站了十一年，今天才知道，从外头看，它这么小。

记：沈小满，欠我鸡蛋三个半。利息，另算。

写到这里，油灯的芯子「噼」地爆了一下。那姑娘抬起头来，看了看窗外的月亮，吹熄了灯，把小本子塞进枕头底下，压好了，这才睡下。

这姑娘姓周，单名一个禾字。石坳村的人，都管她叫阿禾。

小满躺在最靠门的那张铺上。靠门的铺，是最后进门的人睡的，门缝里的风一夜往里灌。他睁着眼睛，把胸口的木牌掏出来，握在手心里。

通铺那一头，靠窗的最好的一张铺，是马小宝的。他的两个家丁进不得山门，傍晚便下山去了，那两个食盒却留了下来，一个空的，一个还剩小半盒。这时候大通铺上一百来个人都睡了，只那一头，黑暗里，「咯吱、咯吱」地响，一下，一下，很慢，很匀，是马小宝在嚼桂花糕。

他嚼完一块，摸一块；摸一块，嚼一块。小满听着那声音，一直听了很久，心想：他晚饭喝了三碗粥——他是新任的「马师兄」，伙夫给他盛的是满勺——怎么还饿？

那声音一直响到后半夜，才停。

木牌是凉的。那条银色的尾巴，一明，一暗，一明，一暗，睡得很沉。

小满看着它，忽然想明白了一件事。

这一整天，从石阶底下，到石坪上，到林子里，到正殿里，它只烫了一回。就一回，就两个字，「左边」。一试它没有醒，二试它没有醒，测灵石亮成一块抹布、满殿的人笑成一锅粥的时候，它也没有醒。

小满心想：它是醒不来，还是不肯醒？

他想了很久，想不出来。

他又想起今天学到的三样东西。一样是他娘的口诀，原来是一个人，头戴九，脚踩一，站得稳稳的。一样是那口空石座，一千个人下河，捞一口锅，没捞着，三百年，石座还空着。还有一样，是林子里那九个脑袋，八个是空的，一个是饿的。

这三样东西，他那天夜里都没有想明白，只是一样一样，都记下了。

他摸出怀里那个红糖包纸订的小本子，借着窗外的月光，翻开第一页。第一页是空的。他舔了舔手指头，想写点什么，想了半天，又合上了。他心想：第一笔账，得是一笔大的，得记得住一辈子。今天的事，他都记在心里了，用不着写。

他没有想到，第二天一早，这本子上记下的第一笔账，是一块灵石。可有一样他想出来了：不管是哪一样，今天这道山门，是他自己两条腿走上来的，是他娘那句口诀摆出来的，是他爹教他的耳朵听出来的。舅舅走到一百六十级，他走到三百级；马小宝坐着滑竿，他走着。进是进来了，进得不体面，五行杂灵根，下下之资，满殿的人笑——可是凭自己进来的。

他对着木牌，小声说道：「现在打不过。他有荐书，有人，有他家的钱。我什么都没有。」

木牌没有回答。

他翻了个身，看着窗外的月亮。十三岁，五行杂灵根，下下之资，练气零层；家里一年五两银子，一个空钱袋，一张爷爷的弓，一套娘的针线；腰上一块发工钱的木牌，胸口一块欠他一张饼的木牌，里头还睡着一个妖王。

他说道：「可是——」

停了一停，又道：「账，我都记着呢。」

握在手心里的木牌，轻轻地，暖了一下。

窗外，外门的告示栏上，贴着一张新的告示，墨迹还没干：

**沉鼎秘境，十年一开。冬月初一，外门弟子皆可入。**
story.en:
Zhou Heng closed the ledger and sighed, saying to himself: "The most important thing in cultivating immortality is not losing things." To whom, who knew. As he left he took a candle from his sleeve and, before a roomful of new disciples, snapped it in two — *crack* — set one half on the windowsill by the door and tucked the other back in his sleeve. "Lamp oil: half a candle a month. Use it sparingly."

Then supper. The outer court's dining hall was a long low building, a row of long tables, a row of long benches, one big pot. The cook was a fat, burly man; one ladle of brown-rice porridge each, a dish of pickles, a coarse clay bowl. A hundred-odd children who'd been hungry all day threw themselves at the tables, slurping, the room full of the sound of porridge like a sudden rainstorm.

Xiaoman remembered the third of his uncle's three rules and drank faster than anyone. His bowl finished, he lifted it and licked the bottom clean before putting it down.

Put it down, and picked it up again.

It was a coarse clay bowl, greyish-white, a blue line round the rim, nothing special; the outer-court dining hall had two or three hundred like it at least. But this one — its rim had not a single chip.

Xiaoman held it and looked a long time. He thought of the four bowls at home, of the seven or eight pieces broken on the floor, of his mother crouched picking them up one by one, wrapping them in a cloth and putting them in the chest. He didn't know what his mother kept that bundle of pieces for. He'd never asked.

Meanwhile, elsewhere.

The outer court's girls' dormitory was in another courtyard. That night its long sleeping platform was all snoring too; only on the pallet nearest the wall a lamp the size of a bean still burned. Under it lay a girl with two little braids and a red nose, writing stroke by stroke in a palm-sized notebook with a freshly sharpened stick of charcoal.

What she wrote was:

The ninth of the ninth. Double Ninth.

The steps. Three hundred. Charged up; didn't sit. Two blisters on my feet — noted: left one, right one.

He was behind, walking, not running. Three steps a breath, like his dad. At step one hundred and sixty he turned his head and looked at the cliff. Didn't stop.

The Luo Writing. When I'd finished he was still staring. Then he got it right. Half a stick of incense slower than me. Noted: his mum taught him. Mine never taught me this.

The forest. That thing had nine heads. I walked over with my eyes shut and touched the bark; I didn't look at it. He looked, and threw a stone. That roll to the right — I didn't understand it; like someone told him something. Noted: ask. Don't ask. Note it for now.

The stone. Me, three colours; they said above the middle. Him, five; they laughed. I didn't. Ma Xiaobao laughed three times — noted: three.

He didn't recognise me.

Mum said: go. Mum said: don't go the same road as him. Go alone and die, fine; go together and die, that's two, bad bargain. Mum said it and then cried. Dad took me the back way; we got here a day after them and slept under the temple veranda.

Noted: Mum owes me one not-crying.

Dad carried me a stretch. Past the old locust, Dad said: "Past this tree, it's not our village any more." He set me down to walk on my own. I looked back once. That tree — eleven years I stood under it, and only today did I learn how small it looks from outside.

Noted: Shen Xiaoman owes me three and a half eggs. Interest, separate.

Writing this far, the lamp wick sputtered with a *pop*. The girl looked up at the moon outside the window, blew out the lamp, pushed the notebook under her pillow, pressed it flat, and only then lay down.

The girl was surnamed Zhou, given name He — one character. The people of Shi'ao Village all called her Ahe.

Xiaoman lay on the pallet nearest the door. The pallet by the door goes to whoever comes in last; the wind comes through the door crack all night. Lying with his eyes open, he took the token out from his chest and held it in his palm.

At the far end of the platform, the best pallet, by the window, was Ma Xiaobao's. His two servants couldn't pass the gate and had gone down the mountain at dusk, but the two food boxes stayed — one empty, one with a little left. Now, with a hundred-odd people on the platform asleep, only from that end, in the dark, came a *crunch, crunch*, one after another, very slow, very even: Ma Xiaobao eating osmanthus cake.

He finished one piece and felt for another; felt for another, finished it. Listening to that sound, Xiaoman listened a long time and thought: he'd had three bowls of porridge for supper — as the new "Senior Brother Ma", the cook gave him full ladles — so how could he still be hungry?

The sound went on till past midnight before it stopped.

The token was cool. Its silver tail went bright, dim, bright, dim, sleeping very deep.

Looking at it, Xiaoman suddenly understood something.

The whole day, from the foot of the stair, to the stone terrace, to the forest, to the main hall, it had burned only once. Just once, just one word: "Left." In the first trial it didn't wake; in the second it didn't wake; when the stone lit up like a rag and the whole hall laughed like a pot of porridge, it didn't wake either.

Xiaoman thought: can't it wake — or won't it?

He thought a long time and couldn't tell.

He thought of the three things he'd learned today. One was his mother's rhyme, which turned out to be a person: nine on the head, one underfoot, standing firm. One was the empty stone stand: a thousand men down into a river, dredging for a pot, didn't find it; three hundred years, and the stand still empty. And one was the nine heads in the forest: eight hollow, one hungry.

Those three things he didn't work out that night; he only noted them, one by one.

He took out the little notebook sewn from brown-sugar paper and, by the moonlight from the window, opened the first page. It was blank. He licked a finger, meaning to write something, thought a long while, and shut it again. He thought: the first entry has to be a big one, one to remember all his life. Today's business he had all in his heart; no need to write it.

He didn't expect that next morning the first entry in this notebook would be a spirit stone. But one thing he had worked out: whatever else, today he'd come through this gate on his own two legs, set out by his mother's rhyme, heard out by the ears his father trained. His uncle got to step one hundred and sixty, he to three hundred; Ma Xiaobao rode a chair, he walked. He'd got in, and not handsomely — mixed five-element root, lowest of the low, the whole hall laughing — but on his own.

He said softly to the token: "Can't beat them now. He's got a letter, got people, got his family's money. I've got nothing."

The token didn't answer.

He turned over and looked at the moon outside the window. Thirteen, mixed five-element root, lowest of the low, Qi Refinement layer zero; at home five taels of silver a year, an empty purse, his grandfather's bow, his mother's sewing kit; a wooden token at his waist that paid wages, and a wooden token at his chest that owed him a flatbread, and in it a demon king, asleep.

He said: "But —"

A pause, and then: "I'm keeping count of every account."

The token in his palm, gently, warmed once.

Outside the window, on the outer court's notice board, a new notice had been posted, the ink not yet dry:

**The Chending Secret Realm opens once in ten years. On the first of the eleventh month, all outer disciples may enter.**

exits.means: rests, ends the day, or asks what comes next
